title: How to keep reading
hookLine: you've read Genesis, Exodus, Psalms, the prophets, two gospels and three letters
last: A TONE, A HAND ON THE SHOULDER.

cards: A lesson a day opens one page. But the book on the shelf is thick, and some evenings you may want more: a psalm before bed, the rest of a story the lesson only touched.
This year the lessons have walked from a garden in Genesis to a few short letters near the back of the book, and tomorrow they keep walking.
Today is about reading on your own, and how Christians have kept this book open, alone and together.

teach.b: Start with what kind of book it is. It isn't really one book; it's a library, written in Hebrew, Aramaic and Greek: poems, laws, letters, stories, songs and visions.
Churches even shelve it a little differently: Catholic and Orthodox Bibles hold books that Protestant Bibles usually leave out or print in a separate section.
So the first tip is a library's tip: you don't have to read the shelves in order.

teach.h: A LECTIONARY, A PLAN, A SLOW PAGE.
teach.b: Some follow a lectionary, a set of readings for each day or each Sunday, so a whole congregation hears the same passage the same week; Catholic, Orthodox, Anglican and Lutheran churches, among others, use one.

Some follow a reading plan, a few chapters a day, through the whole Bible in a year. And some read very slowly. The Rule of Saint Benedict sets aside hours for monks to give to lectio divina, holy reading.
As it's often taught today, that means a short passage, read again and again, until one word catches and stays.
The second tip: read with someone.

teach.h: A LAMP FOR THE NEXT STEP.
teach.b: The letter to the Colossians asks to be read aloud in church, then passed on to be read in the next town. A friend, a group or a church study keeps the book open. The third: some readers find it keeps surprising them.
A psalm read young can sound different years later.
From Psalm 119, in the King James Bible: "Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path." A lamp for your feet, not a floodlight for the whole road.

how: Christians read the Bible in many ways: through a church lectionary, a yearly reading plan, or slow prayerful reading such as lectio divina, often in a small group or alongside their congregation's Sunday readings.

games.q: you've finished a year of lessons, and you want to read more than a lesson a day. what do you do?
o: wait until you have a free month to read it all.
pick one book you'll actually open, and read it with someone.
only reread the verses you already know.
games.why: Christians read in many ways, and any of them can work. the tips here: pick the book you'll actually open, and don't read alone.

practice: Think back over the year and notice which part pulled at you: the stories, perhaps Acts, the story of the first churches, or Ruth, which you can read in one sitting; the Psalms, one a day; or more of Jesus, in Mark, short and fast, or Matthew, with the Sermon on the Mount.
Pick the one you'll actually open, and picture where and when: a chair, a time of day, a lamp. If you pray, ask for an open heart as you read.
